title: Iconium, Lystra, and the Road Back to Antioch
summary: Paul and Barnabas preach at Iconium until a plot to stone them drives them to Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd hails the two as the gods Zeus and Hermes, until the apostles tear their clothes and point them to the living God. Opponents then stone Paul and leave him for dead, but he rises, and the two retrace their route, strengthening the believers, appointing elders, and returning to report to the church at Antioch.
story: The first missionary trip continues and comes to an end. The pattern from Pisidian Antioch repeats at Iconium (synagogue, belief, division, danger, flight), but at Lystra the story breaks new ground. For the first time in Acts the missionaries face a purely pagan audience with no synagogue to prepare them, and Luke shows both how easily a miracle can be misread and how Paul spoke to people who knew nothing of Israel's Scriptures. The chapter then turns back. Instead of pressing on, Paul and Barnabas return through the cities where they had been attacked to establish the new churches, and they end where they began, at Antioch, telling how God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. That report sets up the controversy of chapter 15.
historical:
Iconium (modern Konya in Turkey), Lystra, and Derbe lay on or near the Roman road network in south central Asia Minor. Lystra and Derbe were cities of Lycaonia (verse 6), while Iconium lay just across the border in Phrygian territory, a distinction Luke's wording observes. Like Pisidian Antioch, they were in the Roman province of Galatia. Lystra had been made a Roman colony by Augustus, with a settlement of veterans, though its ordinary people still spoke their native Lycaonian language. Derbe was a smaller town further east. Timothy, who joins Paul in chapter 16, came from Lystra, and he may have become a believer during this visit.

Because these cities were in the province of Galatia, many scholars think they are the churches Paul addressed in his Letter to the Galatians (the South Galatian view). Others hold that the letter was written to ethnic Galatians farther north, around Ancyra (modern Ankara), in territory Acts mentions only in passing (16:6; 18:23) (the North Galatian view). The question affects how one dates Galatians and fits it with Acts, and it comes up again with chapter 15. Paul himself later recalls what happened at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra and says that once he was stoned (2 Timothy 3:11; 2 Corinthians 11:25).
cultural:
The crowd at Lystra calls Barnabas Zeus, the chief of the Greek gods, and Paul Hermes, the messenger of the gods, because Paul did most of the talking. There was an old story in the region, told by the Roman poet Ovid, about Zeus and Hermes (under their Latin names Jupiter and Mercury) visiting a hill country town in human disguise; everyone turned them away except an old couple, who were rewarded while the rest were punished. Inscriptions from the area also show the two gods worshiped together. A crowd that knew such stories would not want to make the same mistake twice. The priest of Zeus brings bulls and wreaths, which were garlands of wool or flowers placed on sacrificial animals.

Tearing one's clothes was a Jewish sign of grief or horror at blasphemy, and Paul and Barnabas use it here to reject the worship being offered them. Stoning was a Jewish method of execution (as with Stephen in chapter 7), but here it happens as mob violence. The elders appointed in each church (verse 23) follow the pattern of Jewish communities, where older, respected men led; the word cheirotoneo originally meant choosing by a show of hands, though by this time it often meant simply to appoint.
literary: Luke builds the chapter as a travel narrative with one long scene at its center. The brief report on Iconium (verses 1-7) echoes the previous chapter. The Lystra scene (verses 8-20) closely parallels Peter's healing of a lame man in Acts 3: both men were lame from birth, both are looked at intently, both leap up and walk, and both miracles are followed by a speech correcting a misunderstanding. The speech in verses 15-17 is short and contains no quotation of Scripture, since the audience has no knowledge of it; it argues from creation and providence instead, a pattern Paul will develop at Athens (17:22-31). The return trip (verses 21-28) is told in summary, and it closes the loop: the missionaries end where they were commended to the grace of God, reporting the work they had just completed.

outline.t: A lame man healed at Lystra
Hailed as gods, the apostles point to the living God
Paul stoned and left for dead
Strengthening the churches and appointing elders
Report to the church at Antioch

doctrines.note: Paul calls the Lystrans to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them (verse 15, echoing Exodus 20:11). The first thing pagan hearers need to know is that the world is made by one God, not ruled by many.

God has not left Himself without testimony: rain, harvests, food, and gladness are his witness to all people. Theologians call this general revelation, God's self-disclosure in creation and ordinary goodness, which prepares for the gospel without replacing it.

Paul, freshly stoned, tells the new believers, We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God (verse 22). Suffering is presented not as a sign that the gospel has failed but as the ordinary road of those who follow Christ.
The new churches are not left on their own. Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in each church with prayer and fasting and entrust them to the Lord, a pattern of local, shared leadership.

words.note: Mataios, empty, futile, worthless. The Greek Old Testament often uses the related word for idols, which are vanity or breath. Paul calls the sacrifices and gods of Lystra worthless things, not because the people are foolish but because these gods cannot give life.

Amarturos, without witness. The word appears only here in the New Testament. God has not left Himself without testimony even among nations that never heard of Israel. Rain and harvest are his signature on the world.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, trouble. The picture behind it is of being pressed or crushed. It is a common New Testament word for the hardships of believers, and here it describes the path by which disciples enter the kingdom of God.

christ: The Lystra healing is a sign of the same power that worked in Jesus's ministry, when the lame walked as the prophets had promised for the age of salvation (Isaiah 35:6). But the crowd's response shows how easily a sign can be mistaken for something else. Paul and Barnabas refuse to be treated as gods because their message is about the living God, not about themselves; the New Testament confesses only one man who shares fully in the nature of God and humanity, and he is not either of them. Their words, We too are only men, point away from themselves to Christ. The chapter also shows the shape of following Jesus. Paul is stoned and dragged outside the city as if dead, and then he gets up. His life is being conformed to the pattern of the crucified and risen Lord he preaches.

hard.q: If God let all nations go their own way in the past, what about those who lived and died without hearing of him?
hard.a:
Paul says that in past generations, He let all nations go their own way (verse 16), and at Athens he adds that God overlooked the times of ignorance (17:30). He does not treat the nations as innocent; their worship of worthless things is real error. But he also insists that God's goodness in creation was always a witness to them, and he stresses God's patience rather than his condemnation.

Christians have answered the wider question in several ways. Some hold that those who never heard are judged by their response to the light they had (Romans 2:14-16), and leave their fate to God's justice and mercy. Others emphasize that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ and draw from this an urgent call to mission. Still others hope that God may save some through Christ who did not know his name. The text does not settle the question, but it does show Paul's own emphasis: God's patience in the past is a reason to turn to him now.

questions: The crowd at Lystra tried to fit Paul and Barnabas into the religious stories they already knew. How do people today fit Christianity into their existing categories?
Paul spoke to people without Bibles by pointing to rain, harvest, food, and gladness. What ordinary goods in your life point toward God?
Paul went back to the cities where he had been attacked in order to strengthen the believers. What does that say about his priorities?
